topic: The Secret Geometry of Primes: From Dirichlet's Theorem to the Approximation of Pi
target_audience: Undergraduate students or advanced high school mathematics enthusiasts

outline.topic: The Secret Geometry of Primes: From Dirichlet's Theorem to the Approximation of Pi
outline.target_audience: Undergraduate students or advanced high school mathematics enthusiasts

sections.title: The Prime Atoms and the Number Line
sections.content: Introduce primes as the indivisible 'atoms' of the number system. Visualize the number line as a long digital highway where prime numbers light up like neon signs. This sets the stage for searching for patterns in their seemingly random distribution.
sections.example: A 'Prime Scout' robot travels along a glowing 3D number line, tagging numbers like 2, 3, 5, and 7 with golden sparks, while composite numbers remain dim.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Building Arithmetic Progressions
sections.content: Explain the concept of arithmetic progressions (sequences with a constant difference) of the form 'an + b'. Use a graphical 'sieve' to show how numbers can be sorted into different 'lanes' or tracks based on their remainders when divided by a fixed number.
sections.example: Visualize two parallel conveyor belts: Lane A (4n + 1) containing 1, 5, 9, 13... and Lane B (4n + 3) containing 3, 7, 11, 15... Show that primes appear in both lanes.

sections.title: Dirichlet’s Theorem: The Infinite Paths
sections.content: Introduce Dirichlet’s Theorem on Arithmetic Progressions. State the core idea: if 'a' and 'b' have no common factors, the sequence 'an + b' contains infinitely many primes. Graphically represent this as the 'Prime Scout' finding an endless supply of golden sparks no matter which valid lane it chooses.
sections.example: Compare the 4n+1 lane and 4n+3 lane. Dirichlet proves that even if we travel to infinity, both lanes will never run out of prime 'sparks,' ensuring a fair distribution across the number universe.

sections.title: The Prime Race and the Bridge to Pi
sections.content: Explore the 'bias' in prime distribution. While both lanes are infinite, there is a subtle relationship between them. Introduce the Leibniz formula for Pi (1 - 1/3 + 1/5 - 1/7...) which connects the alternating count of numbers in these two prime-rich lanes to the geometry of a circle.
sections.example: Show a scale balance. On one side, we place '1' and '1/5' (from the 4n+1 lane); on the other, we subtract '1/3' and '1/7' (from the 4n+3 lane). As the calculation continues, the balance point settles exactly at π/4.

sections.title: Visual Synthesis: Primes Constructing a Circle
sections.content: Summarize how the discrete, 'jagged' world of prime patterns (Dirichlet's lanes) unexpectedly constructs the smooth, perfect curve of Pi. Use a final animation showing the alternating sums of these prime-based sequences transforming into a rotating unit circle.
sections.example: The 'Prime Scout' robot finishes its journey by bending the two straight conveyor belts into a circle. The frequency of primes found in Dirichlet's lanes dictates the radius, revealing Pi as the hidden architect of prime distribution.

storyboard.title: The Prime Atoms and the Number Line
lecture_lines: Prime numbers are the indivisible atoms of our universe.
They appear like unpredictable sparks along the number line.
We seek the hidden patterns within their random distribution.
animations: Create a white (#FFFFFF) horizontal line with tick marks from 1 to 10.
A golden dot (#FFD700) representing the 'Prime Scout' appears at 1 and begins moving right.
As the Scout hits 2, 3, 5, and 7, these numbers flash gold (#FFD700) and grow larger.
Composite numbers like 4, 6, 8, and 9 fade to a dim gray (#808080).
Zoom out and pan right to reveal a dense trail of golden sparks across the line.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: Building Arithmetic Progressions
lecture_lines: Arithmetic progressions follow the rule: a times n plus b.
We sort numbers into lanes based on their remainders.
Primes populate these parallel tracks in fascinating ways.
animations: Sort the numbers 1 through 16 into two vertical columns.
Color the 4n+1 column light blue (#ADD8E6) and 4n+3 column light orange (#FFCC99).
Highlight primes 5, 13 in blue and 3, 7, 11 in orange with gold boxes (#FFD700).

storyboard.title: Dirichlet’s Theorem: The Infinite Paths
lecture_lines: Dirichlet proved certain paths contain infinite primes.
If a and b share no factors, primes never stop.
No matter how far we travel, the sparks continue.
Primes are distributed fairly across all valid lanes.
This infinite supply ensures a balanced number universe.
animations: Display the formula 'an + b' with 'gcd(a, b) = 1' in white (#FFFFFF) at the top.
Draw two parallel paths (#ADD8E6 and #FFCC99) stretching toward a distant vanishing point.
Many small golden sparks (#FFD700) appear randomly along both paths to the horizon.
The Prime Scout (#FFD700) zooms at high speed down the blue path into the distance.
The words 'Infinitely Many Primes' appear in glowing white (#FFFFFF) in the center.

storyboard.title: The Prime Race and the Bridge to Pi
lecture_lines: Subtle biases exist between different prime lanes.
The Leibniz formula links these lanes to geometry.
Alternating between lanes creates an unexpected balance.
Summing and subtracting these fractions leads to Pi.
Discrete prime patterns reveal a hidden circular nature.
animations: Show a silver (#C0C0C0) balance scale with the Leibniz formula appearing above it.
Drop terms 1, 1/5, 1/9 onto the left pan and 1/3, 1/7, 1/11 onto the right pan.
The scale balances and a label 'Result: π/4' appears in green (#00FF00) at the pivot.

storyboard.title: Visual Synthesis: Primes Constructing a Circle
lecture_lines: Straight lanes bend to form a perfect unit circle.
Prime frequencies dictate the radius of this geometry.
Pi emerges as the architect of prime distribution.
animations: The two straight paths from before start curving toward each other.
The paths join to form a perfect white (#FFFFFF) unit circle.
A red radius vector (#FF0000) sweeps around the interior of the circle.
Text 'Primes Construct Pi' flashes in the center in white (#FFFFFF).
The circle fades, leaving a large, glowing golden (#FFD700) π symbol.
